entry: Large-scale [[Wave interference|wave interference]] pattern produced when two similar ruled patterns are overlaid, one displaced, rotated or differing in pitch. The term comes from *moiré*, a [[Textile|textile]] with a rippled, "watered" appearance, historically made of silk. Moiré patterns often appear as artifacts in printing, [[Television|television]] and digital photography, and in [[Computer graphics|computer graphics]], such as when a checkered plane is ray traced. They are also used deliberately, for example in micrometers, which amplify very small movements. In stacked two-dimensional layers, such as [[Graphene|graphene]] twisted to a "magic angle" of approximately 1.1°, moiré patterns induce states including unconventional [[Superconductivity|superconductivity]].

Desert in the rain shadow of the southern [[Sierra Nevada]], in the southwestern United States. The Mojave lies mainly in southeastern California and southwestern [[Nevada]], with small parts extending into [[Arizona]] and [[Utah]]. It is the smallest and driest of the North American deserts, which also include the Sonoran, Chihuahuan and Great Basin deserts. Its typical basin and range topography includes Badwater Basin, the lowest point in North America. Most of the desert lies between 2,000 and 4,000 feet (610 and 1,220 m), so it is often called the "high desert." [[Alluvial fan|Alluvial fans]] called bajadas surround its mountains, and dry lake beds called playas, where water evaporates and leaves salt, lie in its basins. The [[San Andreas Fault]] forms part of its southwestern border. The desert contains silver, [[Tungsten|tungsten]], iron and gold deposits, and supports ranching, recreation and military training.

Viscous byproduct of refining [[Sugarcane|sugarcane]] or [[Sugar beet|sugar beet]] juice into sugar. Also called black treacle, molasses is a major constituent of brown sugar, and sugarcane molasses is usually used to sweeten and flavor foods. It is rich in [[Vitamin|vitamins]] and minerals, including [[Iron|iron]], calcium, magnesium and potassium. First molasses has the highest sugar content, while blackstrap molasses is the darkest and most robust in flavor. Molasses was a popular sweetener in the Americas before the 20th century. It is also used to distill [[Rum|rum]] and as a soil amendment.

Historical region and former principality in [[Eastern Europe]], corresponding to the territory between the Eastern Carpathians and the Dniester River. It existed from the 14th century to 1859 as an initially independent and later autonomous state under [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] overlordship. Founded by Bogdan I, it united with [[Wallachia]] in 1859 as the basis of the modern [[Romania|Romanian]] state. At times it included Bessarabia, all of Bukovina, Hertsa and part of Pokuttya. Its western half is now in Romania, its eastern side belongs to the [[Moldova|Republic of Moldova]], and its northern and southeastern parts are in Ukraine. The names Moldavia and Moldova derive from the Moldova River, though the etymology is unknown.

Landlocked parliamentary republic in Eastern Europe, bordered by [[Romania]] to the west and Ukraine to the north, east and south. Its capital, [[Chișinău]], is the largest city and main cultural and commercial center. Most of its territory was part of the [[Moldavia|Principality of Moldavia]] until 1812, when it was ceded to the [[Russian Empire]] as Bessarabia. In 1940, as a consequence of the [[Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact]], Romania was compelled to cede Bessarabia to the [[Soviet Union]]. The Moldavian SSR declared independence on 27 August 1991 and took the name Moldova. The unrecognized breakaway state of [[Transnistria]] has held de facto control of the strip east of the Dniester since 1990. Maia Sandu, elected president in 2020 on a pro-Western, anti-corruption platform, has pursued membership in the [[European Union|EU]]; the country was granted candidate status in June 2022.

Small, subterranean mammal with a cylindrical body, velvety fur and powerful forelimbs adapted for digging. The word most commonly refers to species of the family Talpidae. True moles are found in most of North America, Europe (except [[Ireland|Ireland]]) and Asia. The unrelated African golden moles and Australian [[Marsupial|marsupial]] moles have a similar lifestyle. Moles eat [[Earthworm|earthworms]] and other soil invertebrates, and store living worms in underground larders, since their saliva paralyzes them. Moles tolerate high levels of carbon dioxide because their [[Hemoglobin|hemoglobin]] has a higher affinity for [[Oxygen|oxygen]] than in other mammals. Each forepaw bears an extra thumb, or prepollex. Gardeners may see moles as pests, but they aerate soil and provide prey for other wildlife.

Insect of the family Gryllotalpidae, in the order [[Orthoptera]]. Mole crickets are cylindrical, fossorial [[Insect|insects]] about 3–5 cm (1.2–2.0 in) long as adults, with small eyes and shovel-like forelimbs. Most of their life stages are spent underground, although adults have wings and disperse in the breeding season. Diets vary: some species are [[Herbivore|herbivores]] that feed on roots, others are omnivores, and a few are largely predatory. Males sing from burrows that open into the air in the shape of an exponential horn, producing an almost pure tone modulated into chirps. In [[Zambia]] mole crickets are thought to bring good fortune, and in Latin America they are said to predict rain. In Florida, where *Neoscapteriscus* mole crickets are not native, they are considered pests, and biological controls have been used. *Gryllotalpa* species have been eaten in West Java, Vietnam, [[Thailand]], Laos and the Philippines.

Base unit of amount of substance in the [[International System of Units]] (SI), symbol mol. One mole is an aggregate of exactly 6.02214076×10²³ elementary entities, which can be [[Atom|atoms]], [[Molecule|molecules]], [[Ion|ions]] or other particles. The number of particles in a mole is the Avogadro number, and the [[Avogadro constant]] has units of mol⁻¹. The mole was historically defined by the number of atoms in 12 grams of carbon-12, making molar mass numerically equal to average molecular mass in daltons; the 2019 SI revision made that equivalence approximate. The concept resembles a dozen, but the number is huge because atoms are tiny. In [[Chemistry|chemistry]], it expresses reactant and product amounts: in 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, 2 mol of hydrogen and 1 mol of oxygen react to form 2 mol of water. Concentrations are given in moles per [[Litre|liter]].

Branch of [[Biology|biology]] that seeks to understand the molecular structures and chemical processes underlying biological activity within and between cells. It centers largely on nucleic acids such as [[DNA]] and RNA and on [[Protein|proteins]], examining their structure, function and interactions in replication, transcription, translation and protein synthesis. The field draws on genetics, [[Biochemistry|biochemistry]], physics, mathematics and bioinformatics. The term was first used in 1945 by the English physicist William Astbury. In 1953, [[Francis Crick]], [[James Watson]], [[Rosalind Franklin]] and colleagues described the double helix model of DNA, which gave a physico-chemical basis for the idea that nucleic acids are the primary substance of biological inheritance. Its use in medicine is called molecular medicine.

Type of [[Interstellar medium|interstellar]] cloud dense enough for molecules, most commonly molecular hydrogen (H₂), to form. Typically 10 to 100 [[Parsec|parsecs]] across, with masses of 10⁴ to 10⁶ [[Solar mass|solar masses]], molecular clouds are sometimes called stellar nurseries when [[Star formation|star formation]] occurs within them. Molecular hydrogen is hard to detect, so [[Carbon monoxide|carbon monoxide]] (CO) is used to trace it, assuming a roughly constant ratio between CO luminosity and H₂ mass. Dense clumps within a cloud, where gravity is strong enough, begin the collapse that forms stars. In 1951, radio astronomers first detected emission from interstellar neutral hydrogen at the 21 cm line. In 1963, OH was detected in the [[Supernova|supernova]] remnant Cassiopeia A, the first radio detection of an interstellar molecule.

Mathematical function describing the location and wave-like behavior of an [[Electron|electron]] in a molecule. Molecular orbitals are approximate solutions to the [[Schrödinger equation]] for electrons in the field of a molecule's nuclei. They are usually built from [[Atomic orbital|atomic orbitals]] of the constituent [[Atom|atoms]], forming bonding orbitals, which have lower energy and hold the molecule together; antibonding orbitals, which have higher energy and oppose bonding; and nonbonding orbitals, which have the same energy as their atomic orbitals. In general, molecular orbitals are delocalized throughout the entire molecule. Under the [[Pauli exclusion principle|Pauli principle]], two electrons in the same orbital have opposite spin. Robert S. Mulliken introduced the terms atomic orbital and molecular orbital in 1932.

Method for describing the electronic structure of molecules using [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]]. Proposed early in the 20th century, it treats electrons as moving under the influence of the nuclei of the whole molecule rather than being assigned to individual bonds. Its molecular orbitals are approximated as linear combinations of [[Atomic orbital|atomic orbitals]] (LCAO), derived from the [[Schrödinger equation]] using density functional theory or Hartree–Fock methods. The theory explains the paramagnetism of O₂, which [[Valence bond theory|valence bond theory]] cannot. Developed after valence bond theory was established in 1927, primarily by Friedrich Hund, Robert Mulliken, John C. Slater and John Lennard-Jones, it is used to interpret ultraviolet–visible spectroscopy.

French playwright, [[Actor|actor]] and poet, born Jean-Baptiste Poquelin. His comedies, farces and tragicomedies are performed at the Comédie-Française more often than those of any other playwright, and his plays have been translated into every major living language. After 13 years as an itinerant actor, he combined *Commedia dell'arte* elements with refined French [[Comedy|comedy]]. Through the patronage of Philippe I, Duke of Orléans, brother of [[Louis XIV]], he secured a command performance before the king at the [[Louvre]], and his troupe received a royal pension and the title *Troupe du Roi*. His satires drew opposition: the Catholic Church denounced *Tartuffe*, and the Parlement banned it. By 1667 illness had forced him from the stage; he suffered from [[Tuberculosis|pulmonary tuberculosis]]. He finished a performance of *The Imaginary Invalid*, playing a hypochondriac, then collapsed and died a few hours later.

Name appearing in the [[Hebrew Bible]], traditionally understood as a Canaanite god. The Bible strongly condemns practices associated with Moloch, which heavily imply child sacrifice. Since 1935, scholars have speculated that the word refers to the sacrifice itself, because the Hebrew *mlk* matches a term for sacrifice in the Punic language; the view remains contested. Since the medieval period, Moloch has often been portrayed as a bull-headed idol with outstretched hands over a fire. The name later came to describe a power that demands dire sacrifice, as in [[John Milton|Milton]]'s *Paradise Lost* (1667) and [[Fritz Lang|Fritz Lang]]'s *Metropolis* (1927).

1939 non-aggression pact between [[Nazi Germany]] and the [[Soviet Union]]. Signed in Moscow on 24 August 1939, backdated to 23 August, by [[Vyacheslav Molotov]] and Joachim von Ribbentrop, it committed both sides to non-aggression for 10 years. Its secret protocol agreed to partition Poland and assigned Latvia, Estonia, Finland and Bessarabia to the Soviet sphere. Germany [[Invasion of Poland|invaded Poland]] a week later, and the Soviet Union invaded eastern Poland on 17 September. Germany launched [[Operation Barbarossa]] against the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941, ending the pact. The secret protocol was exposed at the [[Nuremberg trials]].

Hand-thrown incendiary weapon, typically a glass bottle of flammable liquid with a cloth wick. The wick is lit and the bottle shatters on impact, igniting the liquid. Usually improvised, it has also been mass-produced, as in [[World War II|World War II]] in [[Finland]], [[Nazi Germany]], the [[Soviet Union]], [[Sweden]] and the [[United States]]. The name was coined by Finns during the [[Winter War]] as a mocking reference to [[Vyacheslav Molotov]], whose radio claim that incendiary bombing missions were "airborne humanitarian food deliveries" led Finns to call the bottles a drink to go with his food parcels. The formal Finnish term is *polttopullo*, or "burn-bottle."

[[Chemical element|Chemical element]] with symbol Mo and atomic number 42. The name derives from Ancient Greek *mólybdos*, meaning lead, because its ores were sometimes confused with lead ores. Carl Wilhelm Scheele identified it as a distinct element in 1778, and Peter Jacob Hjelm first isolated the metal in 1781. The silvery [[Transition metal|transition metal]] does not occur naturally as a free metal on Earth. It has the sixth-highest melting point of any element, and about 80% of world production is used in [[Steel|steel]] alloys, including high-strength alloys and superalloys. Molybdenum-bearing enzymes catalyze biological [[Nitrogen|nitrogen]] fixation, and the element is essential for all higher [[Eukaryote|eukaryotes]], including humans. Its isotope molybdenum-99 is the parent of [[Technetium|technetium-99m]], a gamma-emitting isomer used in medical applications.

Coastal city in southeastern [[Kenya]] on the [[Indian Ocean]] (pop., 2019: 1,208,333). It is Kenya's second-largest city after [[Nairobi]] and was the first capital of British East Africa, until Nairobi became capital in 1907. Kenyan school histories date its founding to AD 900, and the Arab geographer al-Idrisi mentioned it in 1151. Part of the Kilwa Sultanate from the early 14th century, it came under [[Oman|Omani]] control in the late 17th century. Early exports included [[Ivory|ivory]], [[Millet|millet]] and [[Coconut|coconuts]]. It is now a tourism-based town with an extra-large [[Port|port]] that handles approximately 90 percent of Kenya's container volumes, and an international airport.

Scalar measure of rotational inertia with respect to a fixed axis of rotation. It is the ratio between the applied [[Torque|torque]] and the resulting angular acceleration about that axis, and it plays the same role in rotation that mass plays in linear motion. A body's moment of inertia depends on its mass and on how that mass is distributed relative to the axis. For a point mass, it is the mass times the square of its perpendicular distance from the axis. [[Christiaan Huygens]] introduced the parameter in 1673 in his study of the compound pendulum, and [[Leonhard Euler]] named it in his 1765 treatise. A body free to rotate in three dimensions is described by a symmetric 3 × 3 [[Tensor|inertia tensor]], whose principal axes act independently. A flywheel's moment of inertia resists variations in applied torque, smoothing rotation.

Vector quantity equal to the product of an object's mass and [[Velocity|velocity]]. In SI units it is measured in kilogram meters per second, which is dimensionally equivalent to the newton-second. [[Isaac Newton|Newton]]'s second law states that the rate of change of a body's momentum equals the net force acting on it. In an inertial frame, the total momentum of a closed system is conserved when no external forces act on it. This conservation reflects translational symmetry and holds, in modified form, in [[Special relativity|special relativity]], [[General relativity|general relativity]], electrodynamics and [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]]. In quantum mechanics, generalized momentum becomes an operator on a wave function, and the [[Uncertainty principle|Heisenberg uncertainty principle]] relates momentum and position operators.

Half-length portrait painting by the Italian artist [[Leonardo da Vinci]], considered an archetypal masterpiece of the [[Renaissance]]. It is painted in oil on a white poplar panel. Its title presumes that it depicts Lisa del Giocondo, wife of [[Florence|Florentine]] silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo, though her likeness is uncertain. Leonardo may have painted it between 1503 and 1506 and worked on it as late as 1517. King Francis I of France acquired it after Leonardo's death in 1519, and it has been displayed at the [[Louvre]] since 1797. Vincenzo Peruggia stole it in 1911, and its recovery in 1914 generated unprecedented publicity. In 1962 it was insured for US$100 million, the highest known painting insurance valuation. The song "Mona Lisa", recorded by [[Nat King Cole|Nat King Cole]], was one of the most successful songs of the 1950s.

Sovereign city-state and microstate in [[Western Europe]] on the French Riviera. It is a semi-enclave bordered by [[France]] on three sides, with the [[Mediterranean Sea]] to the south. At 2.08 km² (0.80 sq mi), it is the second-smallest sovereign state after [[Vatican City]] and the most densely populated. Monaco is a semi-constitutional monarchy, with Prince Albert II holding substantial political powers, and the House of Grimaldi has ruled since 1297. France is responsible for its defense. Its economy grew in the late 19th century after the opening of the [[Monte Carlo|Monte Carlo]] Casino and a rail link to [[Paris]]. Monaco has no personal income tax except for French citizens, and it hosts the Monaco Grand Prix, a [[Formula One]] race. It joined the [[Council of Europe]] in 2004.

Milkweed butterfly in the family Nymphalidae, with orange, black and white wings and a wingspan of 8.9–10.2 cm (3.5–4.0 in). [[Carl Linnaeus]] described the species in 1758. The eastern North American population makes an annual [[Instinct|instinctive]] migration from the northern United States and southern Canada to Florida and Mexico, followed by a multigenerational return north in spring. Western populations, west of the [[Rocky Mountains]], often overwinter in southern California. Monarch larvae eat only milkweed, whose chemicals protect them from predators.

Building or complex of buildings housing monks or nuns, who live in community or alone as hermits. A monastery complex typically includes a [[Church (building)|church]], dormitory, cloister, refectory, [[Library|library]] and infirmary, along with outlying granges. Larger complexes may add a hospice, school, barn, forge or brewery to support self-sufficiency. In English usage, "monastery" denotes the buildings of a community of monks, while "convent" is now applied mainly to nuns. [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] monasteries are called vihara, and in [[Thailand]] they are called wat. In [[Eastern Christianity|Eastern Christianity]], a very small community is called a skete. Suppressions of monastic houses included Henry VIII's Dissolution of the Monasteries in 1536–1541.

Day of the week between [[Sunday]] and [[Tuesday]]. Under ISO 8601 it is the first day of the week. Its English name derives from Old English *mōnandæg*, "moon's day," a translation of Latin *lunae dies*. Historically, the Greco-Roman week began with Sunday, and the [[Catholic Church]] still calls Monday *feria secunda*. The [[Eastern Orthodox Church|Greek Eastern Orthodox Church]] and Portuguese traditions likewise count Monday as the second day. Many [[Slavic languages]] name it "after Sunday," and in North America Sunday is the first day of the week.
